desc:
Half-open intervals [start, end) are painted onto an initially empty number line one after another, in the order given. Painting an interval covers every point x with start ≤ x < end; painting already painted points again changes nothing.

After each painting step, report the total length of the number line that is painted so far. Return these totals, one per interval.

intervals = [[1, 5], [3, 8], [10, 12], [0, 20], [2, 4]]
result    = [4, 7, 9, 20, 20]

After the first two steps [1, 8) is painted (length 7); the interval [0, 20) then swallows everything.
hints: Recomputing the union from scratch after every step is O(n log n) per step. Painting is permanent, so what work can be reused?
Each unit of length is painted for the first time exactly once. If you could jump directly over parts that are already painted, the total work would stay small.

Compress all endpoints into sorted coordinates; the pieces between consecutive coordinates are 'elementary segments'. For each new interval visit only its still unpainted elementary segments, using a union-find 'next unpainted segment' pointer to skip painted ones.
editorial: Collect every endpoint, sort and deduplicate them: xs[0] < xs[1] < .... Between two neighbouring coordinates lies one elementary segment, and every interval is exactly a run of consecutive elementary segments. A segment is either painted or not, and once painted stays painted.

Keep a union-find forest nxt where find(i) returns the first unpainted segment with index ≥ i. To paint the interval covering segments [i0, i1), start at i = find(i0); while i < i1, add xs[i+1] - xs[i] to the running total, mark the segment painted by pointing it to i + 1, and continue at find(i + 1). Every segment is painted at most once, so the total work is near-linear after the O(n log n) sort. An alternative is to keep the painted blocks in a sorted list and merge with binary search, which is simpler but can degrade to quadratic list shifting.
